column4: The panting chargers open a sustained cavalry assault; their forward exertion gives the section's completed charge a direct Quranic scene without relying on shared vocabulary.
The chargers strike sparks from the ground, contributing the hard impact of weapon-like force to the assault begun in 100:1.
The horses raid at dawn, identifying the preceding motion as an actual attack rather than general travel.
The charge raises a cloud of dust, making the speed and physical force of the advance visible.
The chargers penetrate into the midst of a gathered force, bringing the sequence's attack all the way to its objective and thus closely enacting the section's sound charge.
People are summoned to spend in God's way, but some are stingy, and the ayah then warns وَإِن تَتَوَلَّوْا۟; withholding and turning away meet here exactly as the source opposes giving to retreat.

At danger the hypocrites reel in fear, but afterward assail believers بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ while begrudging good; their only sharp weapon is the tongue, exposing hard speech without battlefield courage or giving.
They say they believe and obey, ثُمَّ يَتَوَلَّىٰ فَرِيقٌۭ مِّنْهُم; the ayah directly measures a verbal profession by the action that turns away from it.
When summoned to God's and the Messenger's judgment, a group is مُعْرِضُونَ; this supplies the concrete act behind the verbal-then-bodily turning of 24:47.
True believers answer سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا when summoned to judgment; enacted obedience is the positive counterpart to the turners in 24:47-48.
The pledge is a pledge to God: one who breaks it harms himself, while whoever fulfills his covenant receives immense reward; this directly defines truth as carrying pledged action through.
قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ ٱلرُّءْيَا declares Abraham's vision made true after the submission staged in 37:102-103; truth here is accomplished action, not verbal assent.
The son tells Abraham to do what he is commanded and promises patient endurance; his spoken assent deliberately commits him to the costly act begun in 37:103.
Father and son submit and the son is laid down for sacrifice; this enacted submission is what 37:105 calls making the vision true.
The battlefield command to strike above necks and every fingertip supplies an explicit cutting-weapon action for the section's effective sword.
وَلَا تَهِنُوا۟ forbids weakness after battle and promises the believers the upper position; it is a direct command not to let the charge collapse.
Believers had wished for death before meeting it and are reminded that they have now seen it; the ayah tests a prior declaration at the moment when battlefield action must substantiate it.
Obeying the disbelievers would يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَعْقَٰبِكُمْ, making reversal on one's heels the loss that follows abandoned fidelity.
Despite wounds, the believers respond to God and the Messenger; renewed action after injury is a particularly concrete instance of carrying the campaign through.
News that a force had gathered against them increases the wounded believers' faith rather than turning them back, showing resolve strengthened at the threat of renewed combat.
They return with divine favor, untouched by harm, after following God's pleasure; the return supplies the favorable outcome of the response in 3:172-173.
If the enemy inclines to peace, the Prophet must incline to it; this sets an explicit divine boundary on the section's image of carrying an assault to completion.
Emigrants who strive with wealth and lives become mutual protectors with those who shelter and aid them; giving, combat commitment, and protection converge in one ayah.
Those who migrate, strive, shelter, and aid are called true believers and promised forgiveness and noble provision; completed support and struggle establish the claim to faith.
The command to fight in God's way immediately precedes the call to lend God a good loan in 2:245, placing combat and giving side by side.
The good loan to God follows the command to fight in 2:244; the adjacency makes material giving part of answering the martial summons.
Fighting is prescribed though disliked, and what is disliked may be good; the ayah warns that aversion at the outset does not determine the charge's true outcome.

The command to fight continues until persecution ends, then orders hostilities to cease if the opponents stop; it gives both an endpoint for sustained combat and a boundary against needless continuation.
Spending in God's way appears inside the fighting passage and is joined to the warning not to cast oneself into ruin; giving supports the campaign while remaining governed by right action.
The Prophet is commanded to fight even though accountable only for himself and to urge the believers; personal resolve carries the summons forward despite uncertain support.
Believers must take precautions and advance in detachments or all together; organized readiness supplies the practical protective side of the section's shield and assault.
Those who believe, migrate, and strive with wealth and lives receive the greater rank; expenditure and completed struggle again stand as one enacted commitment.
Family, property, trade, and homes must not be dearer than God, His Messenger, and striving; cherished possessions become the concrete test of whether giving and advance will be completed.
Those who truly believe do not ask exemption from striving with wealth and lives; refusal to seek escape makes action the evidence of their faith.
Those who ask exemption are the doubters whose hearts waver; their hesitation supplies the opposite of the truthful fighter's settled charge.
Voluntary or unwilling spending will not be accepted from the defiantly disobedient; the ayah separates the bare transfer of wealth from the truthful giving represented in the section.
Their expenditures fail because they disbelieve, approach prayer lazily, and spend reluctantly; incomplete inward assent makes the outward gift ineffective.
When revelation commands belief and striving beside the Messenger, the affluent ask leave to remain behind; capacity without action exposes the abandoned summons.
They are content to remain with those left behind, so their hearts are sealed; this gives the settled posture of the refusal voiced in 9:86.
Excuse-makers seek permission while those who كَذَبُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ sit back; lying is concretely manifested as absence from the campaign.
The weak, ill, and genuinely unequipped incur no blame when sincere; this distinguishes inability from the moral failure of a capable person who breaks off or avoids the charge.
Those turned away only because no mount could be found leave with eyes overflowing in grief; their frustrated desire to contribute forms the clearest boundary against cowardly retreat.
Blame falls on the wealthy who ask permission and accept remaining behind; ample capacity makes their refusal the inverse of complete giving and action.
After the hardship and the three left behind in 9:117-118, believers are commanded to fear God and be with the truthful; campaign conduct gives the command its concrete setting.

The three left behind endure constriction until they know there is no refuge from God except with Him, and God turns to them; their truthful repentance marks recovery after failure to join the campaign.
Medina's people and neighboring Bedouins must not remain behind or prefer themselves to the Messenger; the ayah directly forbids self-preserving withdrawal from shared struggle.
Every expenditure, small or great, and every valley crossed is recorded for reward; both giving and the physical completion of the march count as parts of the campaign.
During the siege, hypocrites call God's and the Messenger's promise delusion; their denial under pressure is the negative counterpart to the believers' وَصَدَقَ ٱللَّهُ in 33:22.
Had the city been breached from its sides and treachery requested, the fearful would have yielded quickly; the ayah tests their firmness at the imagined point of enemy entry.

God turns the attacking disbelievers back without gain and spares believers the fighting; it supplies a divinely achieved victory outcome while showing that completion need not mean endless human attack.
Laggards who missed the hard expedition ask to follow when spoils are available; their selective willingness exposes words and action governed by gain rather than faithful resolve.
God is pleased with the believers pledging under the tree, knows what is in their hearts, and rewards them with a near victory; inward truth, binding action, and conquest converge.
Servants أُو۟لِى بَأْسٍۢ شَدِيدٍۢ range through the dwellings when the promised judgment arrives; it stages the severe, effective assault named abstractly with iron in 57:25.
The queen's advisers declare themselves possessors of strength and severe might while leaving command to her; the ayah explicitly frames martial hardness as capacity awaiting a decision.
The queen answers that kings ruin towns and abase their honored people when they enter; it supplies the destructive human consequence that limits admiration of the severe force claimed in 27:33.

The divinely loved people are humble toward believers, mighty toward unbelievers, and strive without fearing blame; like 48:29, the ayah assigns softness and hardness to their proper relations while retaining courage in action.
After Uhud, gentleness keeps followers gathered whereas harshness would disperse them; consultation is followed by firm resolve and trust, showing that softness of manner can enable decisive action.
They give food despite loving it to the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9-11 show this gift completed without repayment and answered by divine protection.
The givers seek God's face alone and want neither recompense nor thanks, making the gift a fully carried act rather than an exchange left awaiting return.
Their fear of a grim day supplies the Godfearing motive behind the giving of 76:8 and the protective outcome of 76:11.
فَوَقَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمِ makes protection the answer to the fearful, selfless giving of 76:8-10, closely matching the source's shielded giver.
ٱلصَّاحِبِ بِٱلْجَنۢبِ names the companion at one's side; that spatial sense directly explains the dictionary statement that a shield is called مِجْنَب because it stays beside the person.

Moses' sister observes him عَن جُنُبٍۢ, using the root for a position off to the side or at a distance; the precise spatial nuance is uncertain, but it belongs to the sense underlying the shield's name.
فَبَصَرُكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ حَدِيدٌۭ uses the iron root adjectivally for sharp sight, preserving the sharpness component heard in the section's hard, cutting iron while changing the object entirely.
The one who brings truth and confirms it is identified with the Godfearing; the ayah joins صِدْق and taqwa, the same two qualities embodied by the source's truthful giver and protected fighter.

Whoever acts righteously, male or female, enters the Garden and is provided for without measure; action and outcome apply equally across the sex pair, limiting the old weapon terminology's strong/weak gender metaphor.
Hypocritical men and women belong to one another, command wrong, and close their hands; the paired sexes share the withholding action that opposes the source giver.
Believing men and women are allies who command right and give alms; the same paired sexes share active giving and mutual protection, reversing 9:67's closed hands.
Fear God as able, listen, obey, and spend; the sequence makes giving part of enacted obedience and distinguishes human limitation from refusal.
The slain rejoice in God's bounty and in those who have not yet joined them, with no fear or grief; this continues 3:169 by showing martyrdom as a genuinely favorable outcome.
The martyrs rejoice in divine favor and reward, completing the passage's account of why battlefield death belongs among the good outcomes.
Permission to fight is granted to those attacked and wronged, with a promise that God can give victory; the ayah joins justified combat to its hoped-for favorable end.
Those driven from their homes are defended because unchecked aggression would destroy houses of worship; it supplies the protective purpose of the fighting permitted in 22:39.
Satan tells a person to disbelieve and then, once he does, disowns him; incitement followed by abandonment is a nonmilitary parallel to urging an action and failing it at the decisive point.
